title: The Star Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: The Star upright: hope, renewal; reversed: hope running low. Love, work, advice, Waite's 1911 text and the 1909 card. Draw it for your question.
image_alt: The Star, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a naked woman kneels by a pool under a large yellow star and seven white ones, pouring water from two jugs onto the land and into the pool.
capsule: The Star is card XVII of the Major Arcana: hope, renewal and calm once a difficult stretch is over. Reversed, that hope runs low and can turn into discouragement or despair. It is one of the gentlest cards, asking only that you keep the light in view. Water poured freely under a great star makes the upright answer a yes.

blocks.heading: What is on The Star card?
paragraphs: A great eight-pointed star shines over open country; Waite describes it as "surrounded by seven lesser stars—also of eight rays" (p. 136). On the 1909 card the large star is yellow, the seven small ones are white, the sky is pale blue, and the numeral XVII sits above.

Below, a naked woman kneels beside a pool, one knee on the grass and one foot resting on the water, as Waite describes her (p. 136). In his words she "pours Water of Life from two great ewers" (p. 136). On the 1909 card one jug empties into the pool and sends out rings, while the other pours onto the grass, where the water runs off in small streams.

Behind her, Waite notes, is rising ground, and on the right "a shrub or tree, whereon a bird alights" (p. 136); on the 1909 card the bird is reddish, with a long beak. Waite says the figure "expresses eternal youth and beauty" and repeats, with approval, the card's two mottoes, "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit" (p. 136).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about The Star?
paragraphs: Waite's list holds two readings side by side. The first is about something taken away; the second, which he brings in with the words "another reading says" (p. 286), is the one the card is known for now: hope and bright prospects. The reversed words describe pride and a lack of strength.

Waite himself did not think much of the hopeful summary. He called the explanations that boil the card down to hope "tawdry" (p. 136), and wrote that to most prepared minds the figure "will appear as the type of Truth unveiled, glorious in undying beauty" (p. 139).

blocks.heading: What does The Star mean upright?
paragraphs: Hope and renewal sit at the center of this card: the feeling of breathing more easily after a difficult time, or a quiet sense that things can be good again. It often turns up once the heaviest pressure has passed and there is room to look up. Faith and a renewed sense of purpose belong here too; modern readings often call it the calm after the storm.

Calm, not excitement, sets the tone. The woman on the card is not hurrying; she kneels, pours and takes her time. That is the kind of inspiration this card brings: steady and generous, with no need for anything spectacular to happen first.
Let yourself believe in something good again and take one small, honest step toward it. A useful question to sit with: what would I hope for if I stopped bracing for disappointment?

blocks.heading: What does The Star mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, The Star can describe hope running low: discouragement after a long effort, a loss of faith, or a sense of disconnection from what usually inspires you. At its heaviest it means despair, the feeling that nothing good lies ahead. It may also point to self-doubt, a quiet voice saying that good things are meant for other people.

Waite's reversed list goes another way, toward pride and lack of strength (p. 286); low hope and self-doubt belong to the modern reading, not to Waite. The light in the picture is still there when the card is turned around; it is only harder to see.
The remedy is usually small. Go back to one thing that has brought you calm before, and let that be enough for now.

blocks.heading: What does The Star mean in love?
paragraphs: Openness and gentle optimism are what The Star brings to love, starting with the kindness you offer yourself. Inside a relationship, the card favors calm, sincere moments: saying what you hope for together, renewing small gestures of care, a bond that feels both hopeful and deep.
After a disappointment, and with no partner for now, it can mean feeling ready to hope again and wishing for a connection that feels kind and honest.
Discouragement, a doubt that you deserve something good, or a lost faith in love itself is what the reversed card can show here. Where could you be a little kinder to yourself today?

blocks.heading: What does The Star mean for work and money?
paragraphs: Renewed inspiration is the work side of The Star: interest coming back after a draining period, a project that feels meaningful, a direction that is calm rather than driven. Steady effort and work that fits your values do well under it.

Money under The Star means recovery and steadier ground after a lean period: bills that weigh less, a budget that can finally breathe, room to be generous. It promises no windfall; it favors patience and small, realistic steps over big leaps.
Turned around, it can mean money worries that drain your hope, or discouragement that makes you give up before you have really started.

blocks.heading: What is The Star's advice?
paragraphs: Step outside tonight, look at the sky for a while and name one hope. Keep that hope quiet and specific: one thing you would like to grow, said plainly to yourself. Then do something small that pours a little care into it, the way the woman waters the land.

blocks.heading: Is The Star a yes or no card?
The Star as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: Admiration and tender hope are what The Star stands for as a feelings card: genuine affection, a sense that the bond is good and worth believing in, often with a touch of idealism, as if the other person were a source of inspiration. Feelings under this card are sincere and calm rather than fiery. Reversed, the hope fades into disappointment, doubt that the connection can work, or affection that is still there but tired. As a person, The Star portrays someone kind, generous and optimistic, a presence people breathe easier around; in you, it is whatever still believes in good things after a hard time.

pairs.text: Hope arriving right after a shake-up. Rebuild slowly, starting with what still feels true.
Hope meets an open heart. Let a new feeling in without rushing it.
A move toward calmer water, with hope as the guide. Keep going, one stretch at a time.
Quiet hope growing into plain joy. Let yourself enjoy what is going well.

blocks.heading: The Star or Temperance?
paragraphs: Each of these cards has a single figure handling water. In Temperance a winged angel passes liquid "from chalice to chalice", one foot on earth and one in water, as Waite puts it (p. 124); its modern sense is balance and patience. The Star pours outward, onto land and pool, with one knee on the ground. Temperance is about blending and finding the right pace; The Star is about hope coming back.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about The Star
paragraphs: What do I still hope for, if I am honest with myself?
What has brought me calm before, and could I return to it now?
Where could I pour a little care today?

faq.q: Is The Star a good or bad card?
faq.a: A good one: few cards in the deck are gentler. It supports hope, calm and the slow return of energy after a hard time. Hope does need small actions to stay alive, though. Reversed, it simply says that the light is harder to see for the moment.

faq.q: Why does Waite's list for The Star begin with loss?
faq.a: His list gathers older readings that disagree. It opens with deprivation, then turns: "another reading says—hope and bright prospects" (p. 286). His overview of the trumps also notes that the card "has been called that of Hope" (p. 26), and that second line is the one Arcana Diary follows.

faq.q: Is the star on The Star card Sirius?
faq.a: Waite records that name but does not insist on it. His survey of the old trumps calls the card "The Star, Dog-Star, or Sirius" (p. 26), and later he shrugs: "it is the star Sirius or another, as predisposition pleases" (p. 47). The 1909 card itself gives the star no name.

faq.q: Does The Star mean a wish will come true?
faq.a: No card can promise that. The Star describes the state of hoping, not a result: it shows that you can believe in something good again. What follows depends on many things no card controls, and on the small steps you choose to take.

faq.q: Does The Star mean he loves me?
faq.a: It is one of the warmest answers a card can give to that question. The Star means sincere, hopeful affection: trust, admiration and the wish for something lasting and kind, with no drama in it. Reversed, the warmth is there but discouraged. Feelings of this kind tend to grow slowly, through small and steady gestures.

waite.quote: Loss, theft, privation, abandonment; another reading says—hope and bright prospects, Reversed: Arrogance, haughtiness, impotence.
